text: Tries: line piece stops on squares that block something else (e.g. f6 blocks a knight mate, g7 cuts a rook path)
Start with simple defences to explore; replace with heavier ones (pieces vacating squares) when refining
Not every idea is realisable: some are impossible by construction (e.g. a rook cannot block a pin by another rook on the same line) or there is not enough space.
Choose the thematic squares so that intermediate steps (tries, intermediate squares) can be differentiated later; poor square choice makes tries impossible to separate.
Pieces need not mate directly: the meaningful guard of a square prepares the mates.
Shift the whole setting (e.g. one file left) to gain space.
Force a choice by a line-blocking requirement: e.g. the key rook must stay on c2-c4 to stop ...Rc1; tries leaving that zone share the refutation, which is a mechanism, not the theme.
Tries by the key piece, each blocking a different White line piece (Rc4 cuts Ba2, Rc3 cuts Bb2); the mate that works in the solution fails in the try.
Defences that merely guard the threat square, answered by mates that merely exploit the unguard, are uninteresting; mates should impress.
If the key piece has no role in the mates, consider giving it a mating role, even though that makes the tries harder to keep working.
Change material to change the play: e.g. one queen instead of two bishops. Vacating a square near the king invites flight-giving tactics.

Replacing two bishops by one queen: the bishops used parallel diagonals (a2-g8 via c4, a1-h8 via c3) which no single queen square shares; the queen must use a rank + a diagonal (only b3 works: diag to d5 via c4, rank to d3 via c3), so the guarded squares change (d4 guard lost).
source: Claude exploration s3, for E. Bourd review

text: A queen near an exposed king brings direct cooks (Qc2#, Qd3#); closing them cost two Black guards (Bb1 for c2, Sf2 for d3), and Bb1 turned the key into a Black line-cut (Rc2 cuts b1-d3).

Random search again failed without a constructed skeleton (dropped the queen, drifted). Reasoning about line geometry first, then solver-checking single changes, found the working mechanism in 3 steps.

Without the solver Claude found key, threat and 3/4 variations of the 2002 half-pin #2, missed the subtle unpin defence 1...Qd6 2.Qd3#, and made a geometric slip (thought Bc4 checks a king on d4: c4-d4 is a rank, not a diagonal). All claims must go through the solver.
A device (e.g. the pin of d5) should play in all thematic variations; in yacpdb 2753 the d5 pin decides only 2.Qc4# (the unpin is a defence motive in Qd6/Sxd7 but not a mate factor).

A capture key that removes the only guard of the threat square AND supports it is obvious. A quiet key needs a new mechanism that guards the threat square in the diagram and is switched off by the key (e.g. key cuts a Black line).
source: Claude analysis s3 (reviewed with E. Bourd)

text: Multi-functional units (e.g. bPf5: guards e4 against Qe4# and stops Se6+) make a setting tight but hard to improve locally; tool test: removing f5 gives 8 keys.

Searching for the key: fix the post-key play first, then look for first moves that produce it (a piece arriving at the same square from several origins, a piece leaving a line, a knight leaving d6 to open a pin). Do not commit to a key early; collect candidates that allow more play, then check what each try spoils. Refutations should be thematic, not incidental.

If the refutations of the tries are unthematic the tries are much less interesting; the try mechanism has to be related to the theme (here the half-pin), and the thematic mates may be changed if that fits better.

Hard scheme: dual avoidance for the mates is not easy to find, and adding thematic tries is rough even after the theme is clean. Order of work: get a clean dual-avoidance scheme first, then add tries.
A shared refutation is acceptable in itself, but it is worse when the refuting move is a random//unthematic move.
A dual in a thematic variation is unacceptable: the thematic purity is gone. Also the thematic defences should USE the theme (1...Sxd7 did not use the half-pin).

Post-key scheme search: a sound post-key position is just 'White mates in 1 after every Black reply'. Testing that costs ~1ms instead of ~300ms for a full #2 analysis, so 4000 candidates/second and exhaustive enumeration of small cores become possible. Tolerate unanswered replies as 'holes' during the prototype stage, then close them.

Content must be measured per PIECE, not per move: eight moves of one piece answered by the same mate is not content. For a half-pin: each half-pinned unit should provoke its own mate, disjoint from the other unit's (true dual avoidance).

A mate that CAPTURES the pinned unit, or that merely needs the half-pinner as a guard for the mating piece, does not use the pin (2.Qxe5# protected by Bh8 is not thematic). The pin is exploited only when the pinned unit, were it free, could capture the mating unit or interpose on the check line.

Dual avoidance needs an additional effect: there must be a concrete reason why the other mate fails after the other defence (the freed unit guards or captures the mating square, blocks the line, occupies it). "The king simply escapes" is a weak reason.

Aim for unity in the defences: here both thematic defences go to the SAME square (g3) and neither captures. Compare the motivation too - if one defence works by line opening and the other by giving a flight, that is a drawback.

Make the defences easy to generate (almost any threat is met by them), so they force one of the two queen mates; then choose the key square as the only one commanding BOTH mating squares. The other approach squares (b3, d2) each command only one and fail to the corresponding thematic defence.
A structure where the queen holds many squares in the mates is fragile.
Choose a threat that also attacks the half-pinned unit (f5), so that "not guarded any more by the knight" becomes a defence.

The underlying motive of a dual-avoidance problem is WHY the other mate fails in each variation; mark it explicitly when giving the solution, e.g. 1...Rg3 2.Qxd4# (2.Qxe6? Rxe6!) / 1...Sg3 2.Qxe6# (2.Qxd4? Kf5!). The KIND of reason should be unified across the defences - a capture by the freed unit in one and a king flight in the other is the missing second layer of unity. Compose with this motive in mind.

Purer motivations, in rising order of unity: (a) a sibling mate refuted by a unit that never moved (incidental); (b) the king simply escaping (weak); (c) the defender itself keeping hold of the line it held before it moved; (d) each defence opening a line for another Black unit. (c) and (d) are unified motives worth composing around.
The point of composing is exploring new exploits: inventing mechanisms, testing them and iterating - not only satisfying known themes.

A half-battery of two black PAWNS is impossible on a diagonal: the rear pawn guards a square that lies ON the pin line (e.g. pawn f6 with pinner Bh8 and bKd4 guards e5, which is on h8-d4), so a White unit mating there interposes on its own pin line and the pin is never exploited. Only pawns on the same ROW or COLUMN work: there both guard squares lie off the line, and a mate on one of them uses the half-pin.

Derived structure for a black pawn half-battery on a FILE (pinner Rd8, pawns d6/d5, bKd4): the rear pawn cannot advance (blocked by its partner) and the front pawn cannot advance (the king is there), so BOTH defences must be captures - a unity for free. The four squares c4/e4/c5/e5 serve double duty: each is both a possible bait (to be captured) and a possible mating square, so bait and mate must be assigned crosswise (d5xe4 -> mate c5; d6xe5 -> mate c4).

Two further constraints found by search: (1) a pawn capture only counts as a defence if the captured unit was essential to the threat; (2) the thematic mates land next to the black king, so the mating unit must be guarded - this is the main construction cost and the reason small cores fail.
score_core must reject dual threats and holes outright rather than merely penalising them: a core with a dual threat (Sc6#/Sf3#) still topped the ranking through other bonuses.

On a RANK the pawns can advance, so the defences need not be captures - and the mate can capture the advanced pawn itself (1...e4 2.Qxe4#). My earlier conclusion that pawn defences must be captures applies to the FILE only.

Method: describe a thematic variation by three independent choices - how the unit leaves the line (advance/capture/piece move), how the pin is exploited (capture prevention/interposition prevention), and why the sibling mate fails (defender retains control/line opening/another unit/king flight/no check). Known problems fill cells of that grid; empty cells are candidate mechanisms to build. compose/motif_space.py keeps the map in knowledge/motifs.json.
source: Claude s9, for E. Bourd review

text: Bug found by E. Bourd: when several Black moves refute a sibling mate, reporting the FIRST legal one hides the motive (2.Qe5? was reported as refuted by Kd3, when the thematic refutation is Bxe5). Classify every escape and keep the most thematic.

Necessity must be judged on CONTENT, not soundness: removing bBc7 from the completed problem leaves it sound and dual-free, but the dual-avoidance motive degrades from line opening to a king flight. The tool now reports that as "needed for the content".
dual_avoidance_after must exclude Black moves that are answered by the threat itself, otherwise non-defences pollute the unity verdict.

Extra (non-thematic) variations are usually unavoidable and are a necessary evil; they merely add extra play. They stop being a cost when they carry something of their own - here the extra variation ends in a switchback mate.
A key by a piece that is out of play is somewhat weaker than usual. It can be redeemed by what it does: this key unpins a Black unit, and that unpin creates an extra variation.

Tries that prove the half-pin are worth a heavier position; dual avoidance can be simple and still be fine if it is unified. Verdict on b2R4/b6p/8/N2pPQ2/2Npp2R/1pPk3P/1Pp5/2n2KB1: not too complex but decent.

Only defences BY the half-pinned units are thematic. A variation from another unit is extra play even when it is pretty (switchback) or caused by the key (unpin); unity of dual avoidance must be measured over the thematic defences only.

Design for a White-king key: the king stands on a line of a White piece and blocks it; every king move opens that line, so the choice of destination is free. Tries = destinations that CLOSE another White line; the key = the destination that closes nothing. Unified concept for the try refutations.

Why my searches failed: with little Black material every try is refuted by a king flight, so the key ends up merely guarding a flight rather than opening the line. For the interference to BE the refutation, the cut line must be essential to the mate that answers one specific defence. The real spec is three-way: defences d1,d2 with distinct mates m1,m2; m1 needs White line L1 and m2 needs L2; king destination t1 cuts L1 (refuted by d1), t2 cuts L2 (refuted by d2), and the key square cuts neither.

Negative result: ~150,000 positions searched across six geometries (wK blocking a rook on c8/c1/d8/e8/b8, queen + bishop + 1-2 black pawns). None gave two king tries whose refutation exploits the line the king closed. Reason: with only two added White pieces the lines are not load-bearing - the king has about five usable destinations and the lines through them rarely matter for any mate. The mating net has to be built first (more White force and Black defences); only then does closing a line cost something.

Order used by E. Bourd for the king-key task: (1) set up the lines and the possible king moves, (2) set up the mates, (3) THEN extend so that the defences themselves open the White lines - which turns the tries into anticipatory closings (a double paradox). Content is added by deepening the motivation, not by adding variations.

Evgeni built the king-key problem in stages: first the lines and the possible king moves, then simple mates (2N5/4p3/1R6/npk5/b5P1/2P1NK2/2P4B/5B1Q, where the tries are ORDINARY shut-offs of lines that are already open), and only later DISCOVERED that the defences could be made to open those same lines - which turns the tries into anticipatory closings. The deepening was a discovery while working, not something searched for.

A third interfering line only earns a thematic try if the square it guards is not already guarded by another White unit. Adding Rh4 pointing at c4 fails because Bf1 guards c4 anyway, so 1.Kg4? costs nothing and is refuted incidentally. The third defence would first have to block Bf1 (on e2 or d3) - and every Black unit that can reach those squares either guards d5 (killing the threat Qd5#) or refutes the key some other way. Verified by search.
Rotating/reflecting the whole setting can create room for an extra defence (here a third one, unguarding the rook mate). A cheap structural move before adding material.

To stop slow alternatives from also solving, give Black a strong universal resource: here bSh3 attacks g5, and 1...Sxg5 unguards f6, so every slow White move fails to it. That forces the intended threat without extra White material.

Necessity must also count TRIES as content: wPb6 takes part in no mate and leaves the problem sound when removed, but without it two of the three thematic tries disappear. The tool now reports lost tries and treats such a unit as thematic, not as a cook-stopper.

Geometric requirement, from the planner: for each try destination t there must be a Black line piece P and a White piece W with P, W, t collinear in that order, and W must be the mating unit for the defence that refutes that try. The key destination must complete no such pin. With W placed on several squares around the king, almost EVERY destination becomes pin-completing for some pinner - so the scarce resource is a clean destination for the key, not the pins.

Searches that failed: 102k rigid positions (Q + 2 knights vs R + B) produced no unique king key at all - the Black pinners are strong defenders, so the position rarely mates in 2; a hill climb drifted to two queens. The pins and the mate have to be built together, starting from the pin geometry.

Order for self-pin tries: first construct the LINES and work out which White pieces could be self-pinned; decide which units those are (here two knights); only then find the mates, and choose defences that make exactly those mates necessary. The pinnable units are chosen before the play.

For changed-mate problems the post-key search is useless: the mechanism lives in the relation between two first moves, so the whole diagram must be judged at once. Changes can run set/try, try/try or try/solution; the reasons range from simple geometry (the same piece mating from a different square) to flight changes, changed guards and battery changes.

Structural trap found in 2Rn1N2/7K/3P4/3k4/pB1p1P2/3n1P2/1p1Q1p2/8: the try threat Qe4# and the key duals come from the SAME resource - the c2-d3-e4 diagonal that the d3 knight opens when it defends. Blocking d3 to kill the duals also kills the try (a black blocker on d3 simply captures the queen on c2/e2; a white one destroys the defences or cooks). When two first-move squares are linked by a line through the defending unit square, the change mechanism and the duals are the same mechanism.

Set+solution is the easier form and can succeed where try+solution fails: in the set version the queen never needs the e4 square, so guarding e4 with a Black unit removes BOTH the immediate-mate cook and the Qe4 duals at once. In the try version Qe4 had to stay available as the try threat, which is why the duals could not be removed there.
source: Claude s16, after E. Bourd suggestion

text: Construction pattern Evgeni used twice: one thematic defence unguards a FLIGHT (which forces White's reply), the second is a DIRECT defence, and extra pawns block Black's other moves so only the thematic defences remain. Rotating the setting helps enforce a single thematic defence.

Set play is content too: a unit can exist only to provide an answer to one Black move. wPg6 leaves the problem sound, the key, all variations and both changes intact - but without it 1...g6 becomes unprovided. Reported now as a set-play filler rather than a cook-stopper.

E. Bourd's construction order for changed mates (session 18): (1) choose the squares and the Black EFFECT that creates several possible mates at once - a self-block is the usual one; closing a line, opening a line, or unguarding several squares do the same job; (2) find the DIFFERENTIATION between the phases - here the mating squares are controlled by Black pawns and each first move (try or key) removes one control, so each phase allows one pair of mates; (3) only then look for a threat and clean the setting. He tried set+solution as well; the try+solution form is what came out.

Same-piece changed mates need a Black move whose effect is exploitable by several mates, plus a second effect that selects among them within a phase. In 8/4p2K/Q2B4/1N1Np3/1pP1k1P1/6P1/2n1P3/8 each self-block (Sd4, Se3) lets either White knight mate, the flight the knight unguards (e3 or d4) picks WHICH knight (dual avoidance by king flight, unified), and the phase picks the SQUARE (c3 after 1.Bxb4?, d6/f6 after 1.Bxe7!). Two selectors, two changed mates, no duals.

A try refuted by a line closing that the key itself makes impossible is a strong pairing: 1.Bxb4? 2.Qg6# fails to 1...e6! (the pawn closes the queen's 6th rank); 1.Bxe7! captures that pawn, so the refutation disappears and the same threat works. The key piece's two captures are the whole differentiation.

Claude's attempt at same-piece changed mates by search (session 18): four skeleton families, ~5M positions, with a whole-diagram evaluator (set play + quiet key + changed mates, holes tolerated) and a beam hole-closer. It found geometries (bKd5 bSc6 guarding d4+e5, wRe4: set mates on d4, solution mates on e5; a reciprocal Q/R change after Se5/Sd4) but nothing sound: the key square attacked by the defending knight, knight checks on the White king, and a complete block cooked by every waiting move. Two hand completions were cooked by queen mates in one that Claude did not see. Missing was the composer's first step: a Black effect that yields SEVERAL mates, then a selector - the search only looked for one mate per phase and hoped relocation would change it.

A set+solution changed-mates diagram must not be a complete block: if every Black move has a set mate, any White waiting move cooks it. Either leave a Black tempo move unprovided (the key's threat then answers it) or make every waiting move spoil a set mate. The search must reject a diagram with a White mate in 1 outright.

Twice in session 18 Claude built a position by hand and asserted it had no mate in 1; the solver found three each time (Qf7/Qc5/Qa2, then Qd6/Qb5/Qb3): long queen lines to check squares are what the unaided reading misses. Nothing about a position is settled until mates_after() on the diagram says so.

Mating squares and the lines that serve them should be close to the Black king; a Grimshaw square in particular must lie near the king, with the two lines intersecting there. Far-off lines are hard to hold structurally (every guard costs a unit).

Fast start for "two pieces defend on the same square": let them CAPTURE a White unit there (e.g. 8/3n4/8/3kP3/8/4r3/8/8: Sd7 and Re3 both take e5). Then arrange the different mates around it, then find the differentiation between phases, then a threat that these captures defend against. A Grimshaw is also a fast start.

Two units defending on the same square (Rd4/Sd4 in 1K3b2/1P1p1B2/3r2p1/Q3P1RN/R1n1k2p/3p1p2/4nP2/4Nb2): the common effect is the self-block; the phase selector is the QUEEN'S POST - on a5 it guards d5/e5 (so Bxg6# and Rg4# work), on d2 it guards e3/f4 (so Sf6# and Qf4#). Each first move supplies the guards its own pair of mates needs; the try 1.e6? does it with the pawn (d5/f5) and fails to 1...Bg7! guarding the threat square.

Necessity must count changed-mate relations lost by a removal, whoever plays the try: wPe5 plays 1.e6? and bPg6 keeps the try phase dual-free; both were reported as cook-stopper / not needed. Fixed: lost changed relations mark a unit as content, and a unit that plays a try inside a changed-mate relation is a thematic unit.

Two pawns that each look removable on their own can be jointly necessary: bPg6 guards f5 (else 2.Qf5 duals in the try after 1...Rd4) and bPh4 guards g3 (else 2.Sg3 duals in the key after 1...Sd4). Test removals in pairs before calling a unit superfluous.

One-knight change from 8/8/8/5n2/3Pk3/8/8/8 (E. Bourd's start): the knight's departure opens the 5th rank for a queen on g5 (2.Qe5#), 1...Sxd4 self-blocks d4 and removes the pawn's guard of e5. Set 2.Re3# needs d5/f5/f4 held by the queen; after the key the queen must PROTECT d4 (2.Rxd4#) and abandon one of d5/f4/f5 so that Re3 fails - that abandonment IS the change. From g5 only f6 (abandons d5) does it.

Why the diagram flight cannot be removed: the queen must reach e5 only after the knight leaves f5, so it stands on g5/h5; from d6/f6/h2 2.Qe5 is mate at once. With d5 covered by any other unit the position has Qg4# in 1 (or Re3 becomes a dual after the key). So in this scheme d5 is a bare flight by construction; the price of a small setting.

The evaluator + beam closer reached a sound 10-unit setting in one pass once the start was the composer's three-unit scheme and the criterion was ONE specific changed defence (Sxd4), not 'any change': 85 raw hits, ranked by whether the changed move gets a mate no other knight move gets, then closed with units that answer the remaining holes (Rg8 for Kf4, Sf8 for e6, Se1 for f3, a Black tempo pawn to forbid waiting keys).
